source: Neroni, Vasconcelos, Crilly (2017) Studying design fixation with a computer-based task (ICED17)
finding: The classic fixation paradigm (open ill-defined brief, example picture, subjective scoring) is narrow. The authors built a bounded bridge-design game with objective measures from the mental-set tradition (Luchins) and found fixation there too.
numbers: 40 engineers recruited, 4 outliers removed, N=36 (18 per group). Primed group made costlier bridges: mean $30,077 vs $27,461, t(34)=3.3, p=.002, d=1.10.
limits: Single small lab study, engineers only, one game.
agent_relevance: Fixation can be measured by code on a bounded task. For S6, a cost or repeat check can detect a fixated search better than a judge can.

source: Neroni, Vasconcelos, Crilly (2017) Studying design fixation with a computer-based task (ICED17)
finding: Mental set showed as a habit of the expensive method. When both a cheap and a costly method worked, the primed group kept the costly one.
numbers: Dual-approach trials: 15 of 18 (83%) vs 8 of 18 (44%) participants used the costly approach; 34 (47%) vs 13 (18%) of trials. chi2(1)=5.90, p=.01 (participants); chi2(1)=13.93 (trials).
limits: Trials are not independent units. Puzzle has a clear optimum, unlike most design.
agent_relevance: A method that worked before gets reused. S6 should flag 'same operator as last time' as a fixation risk when a cheaper path exists.

source: Neroni, Vasconcelos, Crilly (2017) Studying design fixation with a computer-based task (ICED17)
finding: Fixated people worked slower and used more parts, but did not test more designs. Half of the primed group said they designed 'automatically'.
numbers: Time per trial 102.5 s vs 74.4 s (d=.70). Elements 26.5 vs 19.6 (d=.85). First-design cost d=1.06. Automatic: 9 of 18 (50%) vs 2 of 18 (11%). 23 of 36 (64%) could not guess the study aim.
limits: Self-report is post hoc. Small N, one task.
agent_relevance: Fixation is mostly unaware, so asking the model 'are you stuck?' will miss it. Use behavioural signals in code (same structure repeated, cost rising), as in G1.

source: Neroni, Vasconcelos, Crilly (2017) Studying design fixation with a computer-based task (ICED17)
finding: Recaps the base finding of Jansson and Smith (1991): designers shown example solutions repeated their features, even when told to avoid them.
numbers: Original tasks: car-mounted bicycle rack, measuring cup for the blind, spill-proof coffee cup. Numbers of the 1991 study are not given here.
quote: blind adherence to a set of ideas or concepts limiting the output of conceptual design
limits: Secondary description only; the 1991 paper was not opened. It lists later reviews: Youmans & Arciszewski 2014, Sio et al 2015, Vasconcelos & Crilly 2016.
agent_relevance: A plain 'do not copy X' instruction did not remove the effect in people. For an LLM, 'avoid the first idea' in the prompt should be checked in code, not trusted.

source: Sio, Kotovsky, Cagan (2015) Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes. Design Studies 39
finding: Meta-analysis of 43 studies. Examples reduce the variety of ideas but raise novelty and quality. Effects on novelty and quality were larger when fewer and less common examples were shown. One uncommon example helped most. Quality correlated positively with the degree of copying.
numbers: 43 studies. Pooled effect sizes not seen (publisher returned 403); only the search-result summary.
limits: Not opened. Heterogeneous tasks and raters.
agent_relevance: Fixation is a trade, not only a flaw: examples cut variety but lift quality. For S6, give one rare example rather than many, and measure variety in code.

source: Kruger & Cross (2006) Solution driven versus problem driven design: strategies and outcomes. Design Studies 27(5)
finding: Protocol analysis sorted designers into problem-driven, solution-driven, information-driven and knowledge-driven strategies. Solution-driven designers scored lower on overall quality but higher on creativity. Problem-driven designers gave the best balance. Authors had expected problem-driven work to be uncreative.
numbers: Sample size not verified. Scores not seen.
limits: Not opened: repository and publisher returned 403. Search summary only.
agent_relevance: Neither pure problem-first nor pure solution-first is best. Switching by signal (G1) fits, but these data do not test switching.

source: Dorst & Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution. Design Studies 22(5)
finding: Protocol study of nine experienced industrial designers. Creative design is described as problem space and solution space evolving together, linked by a 'bridge'. Introduces 'default' and 'surprise' spaces.
numbers: 9 designers. Per-designer ratings not seen.
limits: Not opened (closed access; one PDF host unreachable). Authors note retrospective accounts of creative leaps may be unreliable. Nine people, one brief.
agent_relevance: Supports reframing as a step. Evidence is descriptive, not a controlled test of benefit.

source: Biskjaer, Halskov, de Rooij (2026) Problem-solution co-evolution research in the DRS conference community (2001-2025)
finding: Scoping review of how the co-evolution model has been used. The corpus is 16 DRS papers. The model is mostly used to link design theories. Authors call for using it as a flexible boundary concept and for tying it to psychology of problem construction.
numbers: 16 papers synthesised. Only the abstract page was read.
limits: Abstract only. It says critiques exist but not what they are.
agent_relevance: Few controlled tests of co-evolution exist in this literature. Treat the reframing operator as a design choice [D], not an established gain.

source: Egea et al. (2024) ChatGPT as an inventor: strengths and weaknesses of current LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: ChatGPT-4 directed two human proxies in a 48-hour prototyping hackathon and finished second of six teams. Concept generation was strong. It gave up promising concepts too early, added needless complexity, and showed design fixation.
numbers: Dataset of more than 100 prototypes. Five human control teams (2 students each) plus one LLM-led team. Rank 2 of 6.
limits: One run, one LLM team, one task, subjective scoring. Humans acted as hands.
agent_relevance: Both failures appear: premature abandonment and over-persistence. A search controller needs a code rule for both.

source: Egea et al. (2024) ChatGPT as an inventor: strengths and weaknesses of current LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: Fixation in the LLM took two forms: it kept iterating one concept after returns fell, and it latched onto the last item in a list of machines. It also forgot earlier constraints.
numbers: Qualitative; nine findings and six recommendations (prompt for alternatives, subsystem-level tasks, human oversight).
limits: Fixation judged by the authors; no inter-rater check seen.
agent_relevance: List-order bias is a prompt effect. Shuffle option order across attempts in code.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI
finding: Chair-design sessions with ChatGPT (GPT-4o) and Midjourney showed repeated familiar features, little contextual variety and sensitivity to high-frequency words. Human Red Dot award entries had more unique wording than ChatGPT solutions.
numbers: 10 novice participants, 30-minute task. Unique-term proportion: ChatGPT 67.4% vs human Red Dot 78.2%. 7 (ChatGPT) and 8 (Midjourney) of 10 noticed repetition.
limits: Tiny sample, one object, novices, word-count novelty metric. Largely qualitative.
agent_relevance: LLM output repeats on open design tasks. Dedupe and count distinct attempts in code before any vote.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI
finding: Users mostly passed tool output on unchanged. Only two of ten edited the Midjourney prompt.
numbers: 3 of 10 asked ChatGPT for the first idea; 2 of 10 modified prompts.
limits: Novices; experts may differ.
agent_relevance: A lazy loop will not vary its input. The program must force variation.

source: Doshi & Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances creativity but reduces the diversity of novel content
finding: Randomised online experiment on short-story writing. Access to AI ideas raised rated novelty and usefulness, most for less creative writers, but stories became more alike.
numbers: 293 writers, 600 evaluators. Novelty +6.7% (b=0.259, p=.001), usefulness +6.4% (b=0.319, p<.001). With up to 5 AI ideas: novelty +8.1%, usefulness +9.0%. Low-DAT writers: novelty up to +10.7%, usefulness +11.5%.
limits: Story writing, not engineering design. One session, lay evaluators.
agent_relevance: Gains per individual, loss at group level. Same pattern as many samples from one model: G4, agreement is not independence.

source: Doshi & Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances creativity but reduces the diversity of novel content
finding: Stories written with AI ideas were more similar to each other and to the AI ideas than human-only stories.
numbers: Similarity to AI ideas +5.2% (1 AI idea) and +5.0% (5 AI ideas), both p<.001, vs human-only mean 82.85.
limits: Embedding similarity is a proxy for diversity.
agent_relevance: Measure diversity with embeddings in code and cap reliance on one generator.

source: Anderson, Shah, Kreminski (2024) Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation
finding: Within-subject comparison of ChatGPT and a non-AI card deck (Oblique Strategies) for divergent ideation. ChatGPT users made more ideas and each user's own set was as diverse, but the group-level set was less diverse.
numbers: 36 participants recruited (33 in demographics), 4 divergent tasks, half with each tool. Group-level semantic diversity significantly lower with ChatGPT.
limits: Small N. Embedding-based diversity. Test statistics not extracted.
agent_relevance: Homogenisation is a between-run effect, not within-run fixation. This is why best-of-N from one model underestimates correlated error. Vary the problem frame, not only the temperature.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Explicit tree search with state evaluation and backtracking beats plain chain-of-thought on tasks that need search. Game of 24 with GPT-4: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%.
numbers: Best-of-100: IO 33%, CoT 49%. IO+refine (k=10) 27%. 60% of CoT samples already failed after the first step.
limits: Well-structured puzzle with a checkable answer, not ill-structured design. Higher cost per task. One model (GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Best evidence that search with pruning helps in S6, but only where a state can be scored. Do not carry the 74% to open design.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: On 5x5 mini crosswords, backtracking and pruning matter. Removing backtracking drops word-level success to 20%.
numbers: IO and CoT word-level under 16%. ToT 60% word-level, 4 of 20 games solved. Oracle best-state output solved 7 of 20.
limits: 20 games only. The evaluator sometimes pruned correct words.
agent_relevance: Evaluator errors cap search gain. Pair search with code-checkable constraints.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: In creative writing, with no exact check, ToT gains rest on a noisy judge. GPT-4 coherence 7.56 (ToT) vs 6.19 (IO) vs 6.93 (CoT). Humans preferred ToT over CoT in 41 pairs, CoT over ToT in 21, and 38 were equal.
numbers: 100 tasks; 5 GPT-4 scores averaged (SD about 0.56 per output).
limits: Judge is the same model family; the weakest-check task is the least trustworthy.
agent_relevance: The closer to ill-structured, the weaker the evidence. Matches G5: judged scores are noisy.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking the model to re-check does not help and can hurt. With oracle labels it appears to help a lot, so the gain comes from the label.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 standard, 89.7 with oracle. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 standard, 97.5 oracle, 89.0 after intrinsic rounds (5 calls). GPT-4 CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 80.0. GPT-3.5 GSM8K keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Reasoning QA with exact answers. Earlier papers that used oracle labels overstate the effect.
agent_relevance: Backs G2: revise only from real output. A reflect-and-revise loop in S6 needs an external check.

source: Xie et al. (2024) TravelPlanner: A Benchmark for Real-World Planning with Language Agents
finding: A multi-constraint, tool-using planning benchmark of 1,225 intents. Language agents mostly fail, and ReAct and Reflexion agents do not close the gap.
numbers: GPT-4-Turbo final pass rate 0.6%; other LLMs 0% in two-stage mode. Constraint pass rates are far below delivery rate (delivery about 89% for GPT-4-Turbo).
quote: Language agents struggle to stay on task, use the right tools to collect information, or keep track of multiple constraints
limits: Constraints are checkable by code, so this is closer to well-defined than design. 2024 models; later models not tested.
agent_relevance: Many interacting constraints defeat plain loops. A program-held constraint list in S6 fits.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Position paper with data. LLMs alone make poor plans, cannot verify plans, and do not improve by self-critique. External critics in a loop help a lot.
numbers: About 12% of GPT-4 plans were executable and goal-reaching in autonomous mode. Blocksworld reached 82% within 15 back-prompt rounds with an external verifier. TravelPlanner about 6x baseline with up to 10 back prompts.
limits: Authors argue a position; pass rates depend on domain and on a verifier existing.
agent_relevance: Backs 'code verifies, model proposes'. In design with no clean verifier the loop loses its anchor; supports G3.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning
finding: Tree search with Monte Carlo rollouts plus reflection beats CoT, ReAct, Reflexion and ToT on several tasks.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@1 92.7% (GPT-4). WebShop score 75.9 (GPT-3.5). Game of 24 (GPT-3.5, n=5 nodes, k=30): CoT 0.08, Reflexion 0.12, ToT 0.20, RAP 0.40, LATS 0.44.
limits: Needs an environment reward or tests. Compute grows with nodes.
agent_relevance: Search wins where feedback exists. In open design, feedback is the missing piece.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Research ideation is ill-structured. Blind expert review judged LLM ideas more novel than human experts' ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers, 298 reviews. Novelty 4.84 (human), 5.64 (AI), 5.81 (AI + human rerank), p<.05 after multiple-test correction.
limits: Reviewer agreement is low. Novelty may not predict outcomes. Ideas were not executed.
agent_relevance: LLMs can do wide generation. The limits are in the next two lines.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Over-generation hits a ceiling. Of 4000 seed ideas per topic, only 200 were non-duplicates (cosine similarity under 0.8).
numbers: About 5% unique of 4000. Dedup threshold 0.8 (MiniLM embeddings).
limits: Threshold choice changes the count.
agent_relevance: More samples from one model give few new ideas. Breadth needs different frames, not more samples.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Judging ideas is unreliable for people and for models. Human reviewer agreement in the study was only modestly above chance.
numbers: Reviewer agreement 56.1% (chance 50%), vs 66.0% in NeurIPS 2021 and 71.9% for ICLR 2024 on the same metric. Best LLM ranker on a related pairwise task reached 71.4% (Claude-3.5-Sonnet).
limits: Different tasks behind the comparison numbers.
agent_relevance: Selection by a model judge in open design is shaky. Use code-held criteria where possible (G5).

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or Artifice? Large Language Models and the False Promise of Creativity
finding: Expert-built Torrance-style tests for short stories find LLM stories much less creative than professional ones.
numbers: LLM stories are three to ten times less likely to pass individual TTCW tests than expert-written stories. Expert agreement: Fleiss kappa 0.41 per test, Pearson 0.69 aggregated; 2,000+ expert tests; 10 experts.
limits: Writing, not design. Expert agreement only moderate per test.
agent_relevance: Open-task quality can be measured only with moderate reliability. Treat creativity scores with care.
